advanced-cache-latency.essentialQuestion: Why must a second-level miss rate be conditional when calculating serial average access time?
advanced-cache-latency.verifiedBoundary: Fast storage close to the CPU is small and expensive, while larger storage farther away is slower; the hierarchy exploits locality to bridge the gap.
advanced-cache-latency.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Performance depends on data movement as much as computation.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: A loop that walks an array sequentially can use cache lines efficiently, while a pointer-heavy traversal with poor locality may spend much more time waiting on memory. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Assume serialized lookup with L1 time 1 ns, L1 miss rate 0.10, L2 lookup time 4 ns, and memory penalty 40 ns.
If 25% of L1 misses also miss L2, the model gives AMAT = 1 + 0.10*(4 + 0.25*40) = 2.4 ns.

The fraction of all requests reaching memory is 0.10*0.25 = 0.025. Substituting 0.025 for the conditional L2 rate inside the same nested formula double-counts L1 filtering and incorrectly gives 1.5 ns.

For 400 requests, use 360 L1 hits at 1 ns, 30 L2 hits at 5 ns and 10 memory accesses at 45 ns. Total 960 ns divided by 400 confirms 2.4 ns. This idealized model excludes overlap, queues and bandwidth limits.
Reference: https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs3410/2026sp/notes/caches.html . This synthetic cache model is not a hardware performance measurement.

advanced-virtual-memory.essentialQuestion: How can the same virtual address refer to different physical bytes in two address spaces?
advanced-virtual-memory.verifiedBoundary: Virtual memory lets each process operate in its own logical address space while hardware and the operating system map virtual pages to physical memory or other backing.
advanced-virtual-memory.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Virtual addresses are process-visible names for memory; translation determines what physical resource they refer to.

starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

reasoningSteps: Assume a synthetic byte-addressed system with 4096-byte pages. Virtual address 0x1234 splits into virtual page 1 and offset 0x234, or 564 bytes.
In address space A, map virtual page 1 to physical frame 9. The physical address is 9*4096+564=37428, hexadecimal 0x9234.
In address space B, map the same virtual page 1 to frame 5. The same virtual address now maps to 21044, hexadecimal 0x5234.
The offset stays within the page while the frame mapping depends on the address space; a virtual address alone is not a globally unique physical location.
These tiny tables omit permissions, page-table levels, caches and shared mappings. Do not infer actual process addresses or a security guarantee from this arithmetic fixture.
Check the documented mechanism at https://docs.kernel.org/mm/page_tables.html . All sizes, traces and mappings above are explicit synthetic assumptions, not measured hardware behavior.

advanced-tlb.essentialQuestion: Why can a translation-cache miss occur even when the requested page is already resident?
advanced-tlb.verifiedBoundary: A Translation Lookaside Buffer caches recent virtual-to-physical address translations so every memory access does not require a full page-table walk.
advanced-tlb.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: The TLB accelerates address translation; page faults concern whether the mapped page is available as required.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Accessing a very large array with poor locality can touch many pages and increase TLB pressure even if the data itself remains in RAM. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.

reasoningSteps: Use a two-entry fully associative LRU translation-cache model, initially empty, and the virtual-page trace 1,2,1,3,1,2.
Assume all three pages have valid resident mappings throughout. The trace gives miss,miss,hit,miss,hit,miss: 2 hits and 4 misses.
At page 3, the least recently used translation for page 2 is evicted; a later access to page 1 still hits.
Every modeled miss can be satisfied from the existing page table without loading a page from disk; TLB miss and page fault are different events.

This explicit LRU teaching model is not a claim about a real TLB replacement policy, associativity, access time or hit rate. Changing page mappings also requires correct architecture-specific translation-cache maintenance.
Check the documented mechanism at https://docs.kernel.org/mm/page_tables.html . All sizes, traces and mappings above are explicit synthetic assumptions, not measured hardware behavior.

advanced-cache-associativity.essentialQuestion: Why can two repeatedly used blocks miss in a cache with four total entries?
advanced-cache-associativity.verifiedBoundary: Set-associative caches map each memory block to a set and allow placement in one of several ways within that set.
advanced-cache-associativity.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: Cache placement is constrained by indexing; associativity determines how many candidate locations exist in the selected set.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: In a 4-way set-associative cache, a block maps to one set but can occupy any of four ways in that set. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.
starter.helper: If a word is unfamiliar, open the vocabulary cards first. Return to the big idea and explain it in your own words before moving to technical vocabulary.

technical.scope: Use the cited evidence to support the verified claim only. Do not infer undocumented implementation details, universal behavior, or current product behavior that the sources do not establish.
technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use an initially empty synthetic cache with four block entries and the block-number trace 0,4,0,4. Addresses are already converted to block numbers.
In a direct-mapped cache, set index is block modulo 4. Both blocks compete for set 0, so all four accesses miss despite three unused sets.
With the same total capacity arranged as two sets of two ways and index block modulo 2, both blocks fit in set 0. The first two accesses miss and the last two hit.
This isolates mapping conflicts at fixed capacity. It does not establish that more associativity always reduces elapsed time; hit latency, replacement policy and workload also matter.
Reference: https://www.cs.cornell.edu/courses/cs3410/2026sp/notes/caches.html . This synthetic cache model is not a hardware performance measurement.

Real processors may have separate TLB capacities and page-size restrictions, so equal entry counts are a comparison assumption rather than a hardware specification.
If an allocation model rounds a 2MiB+1-byte request to whole 2MiB pages, it uses 4MiB, leaving 2097151 bytes beyond the requested amount.

Rounding the same request to 4KiB pages leaves 4095 bytes. Mapping alignment, sharing, memory pressure and allocator behavior complicate real tradeoffs; larger pages are not universally faster or cheaper.

advanced-v06-false-sharing.essentialQuestion: Why can two independent variables interfere through a cache line even without overlapping bytes?
advanced-v06-false-sharing.verifiedBoundary: False sharing can occur when independent data used by different processors resides on the same cache line, causing coherence traffic even though the logical variables are distinct.
advanced-v06-false-sharing.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

starter.plainStart: Start with one idea instead of memorizing everything at once: False sharing can occur when independent data used by different processors resides on the same cache line, causing coherence traffic even though the logical variables are distinct.
starter.tryThis: Use the lesson example as a practice situation: Use the evidence link to verify the definition of false sharing, then identify one place the concept appears in a real system or problem. Predict first; then compare your thinking with the verified claim.

technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Assume 64-byte cache lines and two independent eight-byte counters placed at addresses 0 and 8; their byte ranges do not overlap but both occupy line 0.
If different cores repeatedly access these counters and at least one writes, coherence traffic can arise because the cache line, not each variable name, is shared.
Placing the second counter at address 64 puts it in line 1 under the alignment assumption, removing this particular same-line placement.
Two read-only accesses do not create the same write-driven invalidation pattern; sharing a line alone is insufficient evidence of harmful false sharing.
Padding trades space for possible reduced contention. This address-layout model does not measure cache coherence or speedup, and real alignment, workload and profiling evidence are still required.
Check the documented mechanism at https://docs.kernel.org/kernel-hacking/false-sharing.html . All sizes, traces and mappings above are explicit synthetic assumptions, not measured hardware behavior.

advanced-v07-lab-translate-a-virtual-add.essentialQuestion: Why must a byte range crossing a virtual-page boundary be translated in more than one piece?
advanced-v07-lab-translate-a-virtual-add.verifiedBoundary: Virtual-to-physical translation uses page-table indexes plus a page offset; translation caches such as TLBs can avoid repeated page-table walks.
advanced-v07-lab-translate-a-virtual-add.analogy: Analogy — not literal: picture a workshop with specialized tools and workers. Some resources do different jobs and coordination matters. The real hardware, mathematics, or protocol is defined by the verified claim and evidence.

technical.versionCaution: No version dependency is currently flagged. The evidence links remain the authority for the published claim.

reasoningSteps: Use 4096-byte pages and map virtual page 0 to physical frame 7 and virtual page 1 to physical frame 12.
A four-byte virtual range starting at 4094 contains addresses 4094,4095,4096,4097, crossing from virtual page 0 to page 1.
The first two translated physical addresses are 32766 and 32767; the next two are 49152 and 49153, because the physical frames are not adjacent.
Translating only the first address and then adding consecutive offsets would incorrectly predict 32768 and 32769 for the last two bytes.

The page offset is preserved separately for each mapping. A virtually contiguous range need not be physically contiguous, and absent mappings or permission failures must not be hidden by range arithmetic.
Check the documented mechanism at https://docs.kernel.org/mm/page_tables.html . All sizes, traces and mappings above are explicit synthetic assumptions, not measured hardware behavior.

CPU technique that predicts control flow so speculative execution can continue before a branch resolves.

vocabulary.definition: An event raised when a virtual-memory access cannot be immediately satisfied by the current mapping or permissions.
Page tables store address-translation information used by virtual-memory systems to map virtual addresses to physical memory and permissions.
A page fault occurs when address translation requires operating-system handling, such as bringing a page into memory or resolving a protection condition.
Larger virtual-memory page sizes can reduce translation overhead for large memory regions at the cost of coarser allocation granularity.
A TLB hit can provide a cached translation, while a TLB miss can require a page-table walk before memory access proceeds.
A dirty page contains modified data that has not yet been synchronized to its backing storage and therefore must be written before the page can be safely discarded when persistence is required.
